correctness.rationale: Right multiplication sends a column to a descendant column by coordinate inclusion, so right ideals are precisely compatible column spaces. Each column has one parent, allowing a recursive basis extension: each new vector in column v generates one copy of e_vv A along its descendants, with directness checked columnwise. The ranks at diagonal idempotents are module invariants and recover the multiplicities by differences. For a two-sided ideal, left idempotents and e_tu force each column to be the initial ancestor segment, uniquely determined by the rank. Conversely these segments are stable on the left and along every right multiplication, so all admissible ranks occur. Componentwise injectivity forces the embedding inequality and it is realized by inclusion of the canonical ideals; min/max preserve admissibility. Evaluation at the idempotent gives the Hom formula. Between distinct projective types the Hom blocks occur in only one comparable direction and form a nilpotent ideal, with the diagonal matrix algebras giving the semisimple quotient; this proves the displayed unit count. Passing to the quotient by the fixed parent space gives the Gaussian factor even for a root, and sibling choices are independent given the parent. The chain profile sequences are ballot paths of semilength n+1; the star counts follow by the two root ranks. A maximal vertex above an ancestor gives a right ideal not stable on the left, while the antichain is commutative. These arguments work over arbitrary fields as stated, with the two numerical counting formulas restricted to finite fields. VERIFICATION.md and verify.py were inspected, not executed; the small-field RREF/Hom tests are not evidence of universality on their own.

The broader triangular iso-multiplication result covers a two-vertex chain but makes no uniqueness assertion of the stated kind.

value.rationale: The unique actual two-sided ideal in each module class is valuable in the iso-multiplication problem: it identifies the module embedding lattice with an ideal inclusion lattice, rather than just proving that all right ideals are projective. Over a finite field the branched formula separates the number of abstract types from the potentially many embeddings of a type. The forest orientation is substantive: at a two-parent merge the separate row vectors into a maximal vertex can already span different isomorphic two-sided ideals, so the uniqueness is not a generic hereditary-algebra phenomenon.
